message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree—lions are in the family **Felidae** (order Carnivora), while zebras are in the family **Equidae** (order Perissodactyla).  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the two orders, which sits at the base of the super‑order **Laurasiatheria**.

- **Last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla** – a small, early placental mammal that lived roughly **70–80 million years ago** during the late Cretaceous/early Paleocene.  
- This ancestor would have been a generalized, insectivorous/omnivorous mammal, roughly the size of a modern day hedgehog or shrew, and it gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually led to modern cats, dogs, horses, rhinos, tapirs, and many other Laurasiatherian mammals.

So, the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatherian super‑order, a small placental mammal that lived about 70–80 million years ago.

Or we could say the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the superorder Laurasiatheria. That ancestor would have lived about 70-80 million years ago. So answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the superorder Laurasiatheria, which existed around 70-80 million years ago. Or we can mention the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla.
